strengths: The core idea is original and clearly motivated: a decoder-only transformer that learns, purely from LM loss, to fork or delete residual streams mid-network, enabling adaptive parallel latent computation during pretraining rather than only at fine-tuning/inference time. This distinguishes it from pause-token and CoT-style approaches.

The experimental design is reasonably thorough for the scale: three model sizes (150M–772M), two pretraining corpora (OpenWebText, peS2o), and both parameter-matched (regular transformer) and computation-matched (copy-3/copy-5 filler) baselines, with κ=4L roughly FLOPs-matched to copy-5.

The method sections (forking scores, score-attenuated attention/residual updates, weighted output averaging, partial-RoPE for forks, inference-time budget scaling) are described at a level of detail that supports reproducibility, and the authors commit to releasing a PyTorch implementation.

The analysis goes beyond headline metrics: fork allocation correlates with output entropy (measured both by the forking model and an independent baseline LM), attention-flow analysis shows forks meaningfully contribute to parent-token updates, and CLUTRR qualitative analysis shows forking at interpretable decision boundaries rather than position-dependent heuristics.
The limitations section is honest and specific: wall-clock inefficiency, the top-k gradient bottleneck, and the inability to evaluate at scales where reasoning benchmarks like GSM8k are meaningful.
weaknesses: Internal inconsistency in the ablation (Section B / Table 4): the text claims extended forking is 'slightly worse than forking only in the beginning' and the Limitations section claims 'too much forking results in no further performance improvement,' yet Table 4 shows extended forking achieves lower perplexity (28.02 vs 29.84). This contradiction undermines a key design choice (forking only at layers 3, 7, 11) and needs to be resolved.

Pretraining is limited to only 2.5B tokens, which is very short by modern standards. The perplexity and zero-shot gains are modest in absolute terms, and there is a real risk that advantages disappear (or baselines catch up) with longer training; no evidence is provided about how the gap evolves over training.

No seed variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance is reported for any result. Several zero-shot gaps are small (e.g., HellaSwag differences of well under 1 point at some scales), so the claimed superiority over baselines is difficult to assess without variance estimates.

Results are mixed and not fully consistent with the framing: on BLiMP the method loses to computation-matched baselines at several scales, on PIQA it is roughly at parity or worse on peS2o, and at 150M on peS2o the κ=2L variant is markedly worse on LAMBADA (5.0 vs baseline 8.1). The paper acknowledges some of this but the abstract/conclusion present a more uniformly positive picture.

The baseline suite is narrow. The comparison is only against a standard transformer and copy-filler variants; no comparison to established adaptive-computation methods (e.g., mixture-of-depths, early-exit/universal transformer variants, token-merging approaches like MrT5, which already learns dynamic token deletion with LM loss) weakens the claim of being the 'first-known' architecture and makes it hard to judge the marginal value of forking.
Computation matching is approximate, and the authors admit wall-clock efficiency is poor (raw PyTorch, scatter kernels); a time-matched comparison is absent, so practical usefulness remains unproven.

Presentation has numerous typos and sloppy passages ('attentuate', 'residual whites', 'cocatenated', 'sequneces', 'greatest greatest computational difficulty', a mislabeled duplicate row 'Ours (κ = 2L)' where κ = 4L is intended in Table 1), which, while not fatal, reduce polish and in the Table 1 case create genuine ambiguity about which configuration produced which numbers.

The interpretation of the entropy-computation relationship (increase at moderate uncertainty, decrease at highest uncertainty) is post-hoc and speculative; no intervention experiment validates the hypothesized mechanism.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely novel and interesting: unsupervised, input-adaptive allocation of parallel latent computation via learned residual-stream forking/deletion, trainable with plain LM loss during pretraining. This distinguishes it from pause-token and CoT approaches that require explicit token insertion or post-hoc training.

The method is well-motivated by the expressiveness literature (Pfau et al., Merrill & Sabharwal), and the paper positions itself carefully against the adaptive computation and latent-thinking-token literature.

Experiments cover two pretraining corpora (OpenWebText, peS2o) and three model scales (150M–772M), with both parameter-matched and computation-matched baselines (copy-3, copy-5), which is the right experimental design for the central claim.

The analysis sections add value beyond aggregate scores: fork allocation correlates with output entropy (Fig. 4), attention analysis showing parent tokens rely heavily on forks (Fig. 5), and qualitative fork-location analysis on CLUTRR (Fig. 7), which support the claim that computation is allocated meaningfully rather than heuristically.

The limitations section is honest and specific (wall-clock inefficiency, top-k gradient bottleneck, inability to test hard reasoning benchmarks at this scale), and a PyTorch implementation is released, aiding reproducibility.
The inference-time budget-scaling issue (distribution shift under naive autoregression, Fig. 6) is identified and a reasonable mitigation (proportional/rolling top-k) is provided.
weaknesses: The training scale is small (2.5B tokens), which limits the evidential support for the paper's central and most exciting claim—that adaptive latent computation is learnable and beneficial during pretraining and will matter for reasoning models. The conclusion asserts the method 'allows our model to solve more difficult tasks that require scaling inference-time computation,' but no reasoning benchmark (GSM8k, etc.) is actually evaluated; this claim is unsupported by the experiments presented.

The results are mixed and the headline claims overstate them. Table 1 shows the method does not beat computation-matched baselines on BLiMP, and is roughly equal on PIQA. More seriously, the text claims 'For all LAMBADA and HellaSwag evaluations, our approach outperforms both the parameter-matched baselines as well as the computation-matched baselines,' but the 150M peS2o 'Ours (κ=2L)' row shows LAMBADA at 5.0, well below the baseline's 8.1. This claim–table inconsistency undercuts confidence.

There are no error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance tests, yet several reported gaps are small (e.g., perplexity differences of ~0.1 between copy-3 and baseline; BLiMP/PIQA differences within plausible seed noise). The core perplexity advantage could also partially reflect longer effective context/expanded block size rather than 'parallel thinking' per se, and the baselines do not fully isolate this (e.g., no baseline with scaled d_model or extra layers at matched FLOPs).

Presentation errors undermine rigor: in Table 1, the 150M OpenWebText block lists 'Ours (κ = 2L)' twice where the second row is evidently κ = 4L; Section B refers to forking 'beyond layers 3, 7, and 13' while everywhere else says 3, 7, 11; the paper is unpolished (e.g., 'atrraining', 'intepretable', 'cocatenated', 'attentuate', broken sentence 'approache's ability general ability').

The ablation in Table 4 contradicts the paper's own narrative framing: extended forking is reported as slightly worse, but this ablation is run at only 25k steps on one scale, so the design choice of forking only in the first third of the network (which is arguably a significant limitation of the method's expressiveness) rests on weak evidence.

The concave entropy–allocation relationship in Fig. 4 (less computation at highest-entropy tokens) is acknowledged but the explanation is speculative and untested; it is at odds with the claimed alignment with high-entropy-token literature and deserves controlled analysis.

No wall-clock or memory measurements are reported despite the method requiring scatter/gather kernels and expanded blocks; the copy-5 baseline is described as 'roughly FLOPs-matched,' but no actual throughput numbers are given, so practical usefulness remains unverified.

The improvement magnitude relative to added complexity is modest: e.g., 319M Ours beats 772M baseline on perplexity (20.23 vs 21.22), but at 772M the gap vs. copy-5 is 0.84 perplexity on OpenWebText and ~0.7 on peS2o, without downstream gains on two of five evals.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely novel and interesting: learning to fork and delete residual streams during pretraining using only LM loss, enabling adaptive parallel latent computation without explicit pause-token insertion or additional supervision. This is a meaningful architectural contribution to the adaptive computation literature.

The evaluation is reasonably comprehensive for an architecture paper: pretraining across three model scales (150M–772M) on two datasets (OpenWebText, peS2o), with both a parameter-matched baseline and a computation-matched copy-token baseline, plus zero-shot evals (LAMBADA, HellaSwag, BLiMP, PIQA) and perplexity.

The analysis goes beyond headline numbers: forks correlate with output entropy (fig. 4), attention analysis shows forks meaningfully contribute to parent-token updates (fig. 5), qualitative forking-location analysis on CLUTTR (fig. 7), and the autoregression budget-scaling issue is identified and addressed with a 'rolling top-k' fix (fig. 6). This supports the claim that computation is genuinely adaptively allocated rather than exploiting a trivial heuristic.

A dedicated limitations section honestly discusses wall-clock inefficiency, the top-k gradient bottleneck, and inability to evaluate reasoning benchmarks at scale. Hyperparameters and topology are documented in appendices, and code release is promised, aiding reproducibility.
The perplexity claim that a 319M Thoughtbubbles model beats a 772M baseline, if robust, is a notable empirical result.
weaknesses: No error bars, seeds, or significance testing anywhere. Perplexity gaps between methods can be small (e.g., 150M OpenWebText: 23.19 vs 23.78 vs Copy-5's 24.40), and zero-shot deltas are often within plausible run-to-run variance (e.g., PIQA and BLiMP rows flip between baselines and the proposed method). Single-run results weaken the central empirical claims.

No comparison against actual adaptive-computation baselines (e.g., Mixture-of-Depths, ACT, early-exit/recurrent-depth methods), despite citing them extensively. The only 'adaptive' comparison is the non-adaptive copy baseline, so the claim of advantage over adaptive approaches is asserted, not demonstrated.

Internal inconsistencies suggest insufficient polish and raise correctness concerns: Table 1 lists 'Ours (κ = 2L)' twice for 150M OpenWebText (the second is presumably κ = 4L); Table 4's text says extended forking is 'slightly worse' but reports lower (better) perplexity (28.02 vs 29.84); the text refers to forking at 'layers 3, 7, and 13' in Appendix B vs '3, 7, and 11' elsewhere; multiple typos ('attentuate', 'residual whites', 'cocatenated', 'to the to the left').

The claim of 'first-known architecture' for unsupervised dynamic allocation of latent parallel computation is overstated relative to cited prior work (Herel & Mikolov, Sun et al. 2025, MoEUT-style approaches), and the positioning against these closest relatives is not empirically tested.

The experimental scale (2.5B tokens, ≤772M params) limits evidence for the paper's aspirational claims about reasoning: the gains are on perplexity and relatively easy zero-shot tasks, and the authors themselves concede GSM8k-style reasoning cannot be measured. The connection to 'unify train and test-time behavior for reasoning models' remains speculative.

Wall-clock/computation efficiency is not measured; the method's FLOPs accounting is only roughly characterized ('roughly FLOPs-matched against copy-5'), making the cost-benefit of the added forking machinery hard to assess.

Because original tokens can never be deleted (forced keep score of 1) and forked tokens get extra residual capacity, one cannot fully rule out that gains come from added capacity rather than adaptive allocation; the copy baseline partially controls for this but the adaptive-vs-static distinction would benefit from a matched static-fork ablation.

strengths: The core idea is original and appealing: a decoder-only transformer that learns, purely from the LM loss, to fork or delete residual streams to create 'bubbles' of latent parallel computation. This addresses a real gap relative to pause-token / CoT-style methods that require fixed, manually designed token insertions and cannot allocate computation adaptively during pretraining.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive for an architecture paper: parameter-matched and computation-matched baselines (duplicated filler tokens, Copy-3/Copy-5), scales from 150M to 1.9B, multiple zero-shot benchmarks (LAMBADA, HellaSwag, BLiMP, ARC, PIQA), GSM8K after mid-training, and a scaling-suite perplexity analysis across two corpora.

Useful ablations clarify which components matter: removing the attention/value masking by cumulative scores catastrophically degrades performance (Table 7), keeping only the rightmost residual instead of averaging hurts (Table 6), and extended forking at deeper layers gives only marginal gains (Table 8). Wall-clock timing (Table 5) shows the method is faster than simply doubling block size.

Good interpretability analysis: forks correlate with high-entropy tokens as measured by both the forking model and an independently trained baseline LM (Figure 5), and forking locations align with coreference boundaries on CLUTRR (Figure 7), supporting the claim that computation is allocated to genuinely difficult regions rather than a positional heuristic.

The autoregression/distribution-shift problem is identified and a concrete mitigation (ratio-scaled 'dynamic forking', Section G.1) is proposed and validated (Figure 6). Both PyTorch and Jax implementations are released, and hyperparameters are documented, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The headline claims are overstated relative to the evidence. Contribution 2 claims the model 'performs better in all zero-shot evals as well as GSM8K pass@1 using only half of the training token budget,' but Table 1 shows ours-at-20B losing to baseline-at-40B on ARC-Challenge (24.50 vs 26.17) and essentially tying on GSM8K (31.50 vs 31.46) and LAMBADA (39.32 vs 39.15). Differences of this magnitude are within noise for single runs with no error bars or significance testing, yet the abstract and conclusion lean on them heavily.

GSM8K is a centerpiece claim, but the mid-training recipe includes 40% GSM8K-aug synthetic data, creating a training/evaluation overlap; zero-shot pass@1 of ~31-32% is modest and the 40B-vs-40B gap (32.10 vs 31.46) is marginal. A fair-comparison setting without task-targeted augmentation is needed to substantiate the reasoning claims.

Missing comparison to stronger adaptive-compute baselines. The paper cites Mixture-of-Depths (Raposo et al., 2024), ACT, and related dynamic-depth/merging methods but evaluates only against a plain GPT-2 baseline and naive residual-copying models. Without at least one state-of-the-art adaptive-computation baseline trained under the same recipe, the contribution's relative value is hard to gauge.

The 'first-known architecture' framing (Contribution 1) is too strong given the large adaptive-computation literature (mixture-of-depths, universal transformers, token merging); the novelty should be scoped to unsupervised *parallel stream forking* trained with vanilla LM loss.

Presentation is rough and occasionally confusing: Figure 2 is dense and hard to parse; there are two appendix sections labeled 'E'; Table 2 contains a duplicated row label ('Ours (κ = 2L)' twice for 150M/OpenWebText, one presumably κ = 4L); and there are numerous typos ('cocatenated', 'residual whites', 'attentuate', 'corfers', 'sequneces'). Notation (N vs κ vs L) requires careful effort to follow.

The fixed forking-layer placement at layers 3, 7, 11 'irrespective of N_layers' (Appendix A) is a significant design choice, and the paper's own ablation (Table 8) shows extended forking is better (28.02 vs 29.84 perplexity), which somewhat undercuts the main configuration used in all headline results; the proposed mitigation is only sketched.

Some analyses are qualitative or thin: the entropy-allocation result (Figure 5) lacks a quantitative correlation measure; the 'reduce computation at highest uncertainty' concavity finding is only hypothesized; and attention-allocation analysis (Figure 4) is single-sample/box-plot level rather than aggregate.

strengths: The core idea — unsupervised, input-adaptive parallel computation learned purely from language modeling loss via residual stream forking/deletion — is original and addresses a genuine limitation of pause-token and CoT approaches, which cannot allocate compute during pretraining or adapt to the input.

The evaluation is unusually substantial for an architecture paper: pretraining at multiple scales (150M–1.9B), two pretraining corpora, both parameter-matched and computation-inspired baselines, wall-clock timing measurements (Appendix B), and component ablations (Tables 6–8).

The analysis of fork allocation is a genuine strength: correlating fork counts with output entropy (Figure 5), including entropy measured by an independently trained decoder LM, and qualitative analysis on CLUTRR vs. OpenWebText (Figure 7) provide evidence that the mechanism allocates computation at interpretable, difficulty-related locations rather than via a trivial heuristic.

Honest negative findings are reported, e.g., the concave entropy–allocation relationship (Section 5), reduced BLiMP gains against computation-matched baselines, the autoregressive distribution-shift problem and its mitigation (Figure 6, Section G.1), and the gradient-signal ablation showing attention masking is essential (Table 7).
Code releases in both PyTorch and Jax improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: The headline claim — 'outperforms the baseline using half of the training token budget' — is conflated with compute. With κ = 2L, per-token compute roughly doubles, so 20B tokens of Thoughtbubbles is approximately compute-parity with 40B tokens of baseline, not a 'generous lower bound.' The wall-clock table in Appendix B actually shows the method is ~40% slower per step than baseline (327ms vs. 234ms), and the 380ms 'Baseline (2L)' figure does not clarify the compute accounting used in the main results. The compute framing needs to be far more rigorous for the central efficiency claim to be supported.

Baseline selection is weak. The only adaptive-computation comparisons are trivial duplicated filler tokens (Copy-3/Copy-5); no comparison is made to genuinely adaptive baselines such as Mixture-of-Depths (Raposo et al., 2024), Universal Transformer-style recurrence (Dehghani et al., 2019), or ACT (Graves, 2016), all of which are discussed in related work. The claim of 'first-known architecture' and of dominance over 'non-adaptive parallel computation approaches' is therefore under-tested.

The scaling claims are inconsistently supported: the abstract asserts results hold 'from 150M to 1.9B,' but Table 1 covers only 1.9B while the scaling suite (Table 2) stops at 772M with only 2.5B tokens; the striking claim that a 319M model beats the 772M baseline appears only in a figure and is not statistically substantiated.

No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; several headline margins are small (e.g., GSM8K 31.50 at half budget vs. 31.46 baseline at full budget — described as 'competitive' but within plausible noise; ARC-Challenge 24.50 vs. 26.17 computation-matched baseline at full budget, which actually favors the baseline).

Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track submission: two consecutive appendices are both labeled 'E' (Analysis of Forking Locations; Position Encoding), Table 2 lists 'Ours (κ = 2L)' twice for the 150M row where the second should be κ = 4L, and there are numerous typos ('residual whites,' 'corfers,' 'sequneces,' 'attentuate'). Section D is referenced both for forking-layer placement and overforking. These errors undermine confidence in the overall care taken.

The wall-clock and 'expanded size' accounting in Tables 4–5 is difficult to reconcile: the 1.9B baseline has expanded size 512 while Ours is 1024, and Copy-5 is 2560, yet these are all described as 'parameter-matched' comparisons — the differing compute costs across rows are not consistently handled in the interpretation of Table 2.

There is no dedicated limitations section; significant open issues (e.g., hard top-k blocking gradients for early high-score tokens, the need for inference-time budget rescaling, fixed-context block size of 512) are only surfaced obliquely in appendices.

The GSM8K result relies on a mid-training mixture containing 40% synthetic math reasoning data, and the setup differs between the 1.9B experiment (40B tokens, WSD) and the scaling suite (2.5B tokens, cosine decay), making cross-experiment comparisons harder to interpret.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely novel and interesting: an architecture that learns to fork and delete parallel residual streams purely from the LM loss during pretraining, without auxiliary supervision or hand-designed token insertions. This cleanly distinguishes the method from pause-token, CoT, and depth-recurrence approaches.

The evaluation effort is substantial for an architecture paper: pretraining at real scale (1.9B params, 40B tokens) with a two-stage WSD recipe, plus a 150M-772M scaling suite, with both parameter-matched and computation-matched baselines (copy-3, copy-5).

Key design decisions are ablated: removing the attention/residual score attenuation catastrophically degrades performance (Table 7, 3.90 vs 3.17), output averaging beats rightmost-only decoding (Table 6), and extended forking gives only modest gains (Table 8), which together support the paper's mechanistic story for how the forking scores get trained.

The autoregression distribution-shift issue (fixed vs. dynamic forking, Figure 6) is honestly identified and addressed with the inference-time budget scaling of Section G.1, and all reported results use the corrected procedure.

Wall-clock timing (Table 5) shows the approach is faster than a 2x-block-size baseline, supporting a compute-based (not just token-based) efficiency argument, and code is released in both PyTorch and Jax, aiding reproducibility.

The interpretability analyses (attention allocation in Figure 4, entropy-correlated forking in Figure 5, CLUTTR forking locations in Figure 7) provide converging evidence that the learned forking is meaningful rather than a positional heuristic.
weaknesses: Evaluation red flags undermine confidence in the results: zero-shot ARC-Challenge scores of 24.50-26.17 are at or below 4-way random chance, LAMBADA scores of 39-44 are unusually low, and BLiMP differences between models are tiny (77-82 range) and inconsistent in direction across scales/datasets. This suggests either very weak models where such benchmarks are noisy, or implementation issues in the eval harness; neither is investigated, and no error bars or multiple seeds are provided for any result.

The headline 'half the training budget' framing is generous rather than rigorous: the fairest comparison in Table 1 is Ours@40B vs Baseline@40B, and the 20B-vs-40B contrast is presented as a 'lower bound.' The abstract leads with the half-budget claim, which oversells what the table shows; additionally, some gains (e.g., GSM8K 32.10 vs 31.46) are within plausible seed noise.

The 'first-known architecture' novelty claim is overstated: adaptive computation time (Graves, 2016) and other adaptive-depth methods are also trained with only the task/LM loss; the honest differentiator is parallel latent residual-stream forking during pretraining, not unsupervised adaptivity per se. Comparisons against actual adaptive-computation baselines (e.g., Mixture-of-Depths, ACT-style recurrence, or end-to-end trained pause tokens following Goyal et al. 2024) are absent; copy-3/copy-5 are non-adaptive controls only.

The manuscript contains numerous typos and inconsistencies that suggest insufficient proofreading: 'residual whites' (eq. 9, writes), 'corfers' (confers), 'sequneces', 'syntax matches' (tasks?), a doubled 'ability general ability' in Appendix G, layer placement stated as 3/7/11 in the main text but '3, 7, and 13' in Appendix D, and notation slips in equations (e.g., eq. 8 '+1 log', superscript mismatch between k and f in eq. 11).

The wall-clock advantage is modest and partially contradicts the efficiency narrative: Ours is ~40% slower than the plain baseline (327ms vs 234ms) and only beats the 2L baseline (380ms); the 'competitive timing-based advantage' claim rests on combining this with the half-token result, which itself is questioned above.

Analysis of the 'reduce computation at highest uncertainty' finding (concave relationship in Figure 5) is speculative and untested; the CLUTTR/position analyses are qualitative on single samples, and no significance or aggregate statistics accompany them.

GSM8K results are weak in absolute terms (~32% zero-shot) and the mid-training mix is 40% GSM8K-aug, so the 'competitive GSM8K' contribution is narrow; the practical significance of the gains on general zero-shot evals at 1.9B scale remains modest relative to the added architectural complexity.
